mainEntity.name: Why does my crown feel raised when I bite down?

acceptedAnswer.text: A crown that feels raised is typically due to a "high bite," where the crown sits marginally above the ideal occlusal contact point. This is a common and easily addressed issue. Your dentist can gently adjust the crown surface during a short appointment to bring it into the correct position. If left uncorrected, a persistently high bite can cause soreness, jaw discomfort, and inflammation in the supporting tissues around the tooth.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to adjust to a new dental crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most patients adapt to a new dental crown within a few days to two weeks. During this period, mild sensitivity or a feeling of unfamiliarity is common as the surrounding gum tissue settles and the brain recalibrates to the new bite position. If discomfort is significant, worsening, or persists beyond two weeks, it is advisable to contact your dental practice for a follow-up appointment to assess whether a bite adjustment or further investigation is needed.

mainEntity.name: Can a crown cause pain when chewing years after it was fitted?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it is possible for a crown to begin causing discomfort years after placement. This may occur due to changes in the underlying tooth (such as decay at the margins or root complications), loosening of the crown cement, gum recession, or changes in the bite over time. New pain or sensitivity around an established crown warrants a dental assessment, as catching any underlying changes early generally leads to more straightforward management.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if there is decay under my dental crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Decay beneath a crown is not always immediately obvious to patients, as it develops at the margin between the crown and the tooth — often at or just below the gum line. Symptoms may include sensitivity, a subtle ache, or discomfort when eating sweet or very cold foods. In many cases, early marginal decay is identified during routine dental examinations using dental probes and X-rays before significant symptoms develop, reinforcing the importance of regular check-ups.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to continue eating hard foods if my crown feels odd?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your crown has only recently been placed and you are in the early adjustment period, it is reasonable to favour softer foods temporarily and report any persistent concerns to your dentist. If your crown has been in place for some time and has only recently begun to feel different, it would be advisable to seek a dental assessment before continuing to place significant chewing forces on the tooth, in order to rule out any structural or tissue changes that may require attention.

mainEntity.name: Can teeth grinding damage a dental crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Bruxism (tooth grinding and clenching) generates forces considerably higher than those produced during normal chewing, and this can affect crown integrity over time. Depending on the crown material, this may cause chipping, wear, or fracture. It can also contribute to changes in bite alignment. If you are aware that you grind your teeth, discussing this with your dentist is important, as a protective occlusal splint may help extend the lifespan of your crowns and protect your remaining natural teeth.
